method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Start CPR in any infant or child who is unresponsive and not breathing normally. A pulse check must not delay it.**
claims.source_text: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) should be commenced in an infant or child who is unresponsive and not breathing normally, pulse check should not delay commencement of CPR
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Let the rhythm direct management, and consider ECPR/ECMO early.**
claims.source_text: Ongoing management should be directed by the cardiac rhythm identified … Early consideration of ECPR/ECMO: contact appropriate services as per local procedures
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Most paediatric arrests are from hypoxia or hypotension**, and most initial rhythms are non-shockable (severe bradycardia, asystole, PEA). **VF and pulseless VT are about 15%.**
claims.source_text: Most arrests in children are due to hypoxia or hypotension … Most common initial arrest rhythms in children are non-shockable: severe bradycardia, asystole, and pulseless electrical activity (PEA) … Shockable rhythms: ventricular fibrillation (VF) and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VT), are approximately 15% of initial arrest rhythms
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Traumatic cardiac arrest is outside this guideline.** Cardiac surgery, drowning, sepsis, pulmonary hypertension and toxins also need a specific approach (Poisons 13 11 26).
claims.source_text: Cardiac arrest following major trauma (traumatic cardiac arrest) is a unique situation which is outside the scope of this guideline … Specific conditions require a specific approach to cardiopulmonary resuscitation, such as Trauma (ANZCOR Traumatic cardiac arrest) Cardiac surgery Drowning Sepsis Pulmonary hypertension Toxins (National Poisons Centre 13 11 26)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Check for danger, send for help early** (hospital emergency team; consider early retrieval contact), and **allocate roles:** team leader · airway · circulation · compressions · defibrillator operator · scribe/timekeeper · family support.
claims.source_text: Assess environment for danger, ensuring staff and observer safety … Send for help early: activate hospital emergency response team and consider early contact with local paediatric retrieval service … Early allocation of roles can optimise resuscitation (if personnel available): team leader airway nurse and doctor circulation nurse and doctor cardiac compression personnel defibrillator operator scribe + timekeeper with stopwatch staff member dedicated to family support
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Airway:** infant neutral, child sniffing position; head-tilt chin-lift or jaw thrust; suction under direct vision; oro/nasopharyngeal airway for obstruction.
claims.source_text: Optimise head position - infant: neutral position, child: sniffing position Open the airway - head-tilt, chin-lift or jaw thrust Suction secretions/blood/vomit under direct vision Consider oro/nasopharyngeal airway for upper airway obstruction
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Not breathing: two initial breaths by bag-valve-mask with 100% oxygen**, then continue BVM ventilation — two-person technique as standard.
claims.source_text: If the child is not breathing, provide two initial breaths via bag valve mask (BVM) using 100% oxygen, and continue BVM ventilation as needed Use 2-person technique as standard (if enough personnel)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Intubate only if proficient and without delaying other resuscitation.** If intubated, **use continuous waveform ETCO2** to confirm ventilation, detect non-tracheal placement or dislodgement, and spot ROSC.
claims.source_text: Intubate if necessary (should be performed by proficient personnel and should not delay other resuscitation efforts … If intubated, continuous wave-form end-tidal CO2 monitoring should be used to: ensure adequacy of ventilation identify non-tracheal intubation warn of accidental extubation during CPR monitor for return of spontaneous circulation
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Pulse checks are unreliable. Do not delay compressions if you cannot feel a central pulse within 10 seconds.** No pulse, **pulse below 60 in an infant**, or unsure: compress.
claims.source_text: Checking for a central pulse (brachial, femoral, carotid) is difficult and unreliable as a sole marker for commencing compressions Do not delay compressions if a central pulse cannot be palpated in less than 10 seconds … If no pulse, slow pulse (<60 in an infant) or unsure, continue CPR and start chest compressions
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Apply pads and identify the rhythm as soon as possible. Intraosseous access is recommended** if IV access is not already in place.
claims.source_text: Apply defibrillation pads and determine the cardiac rhythm as soon as possible: shockable or non-shockable … Gain IV access: intraosseous access is recommended if peripheral or central IV access is not already in place
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Rate 100–120/min for all ages; ratio 15:2.** Intubated: continuous compressions at 100–120 with **10 breaths/min**.
claims.source_text: Rate for all ages 100-120 bpm CPR ratio 15 compressions:2 breaths If the child is intubated, compressions continue at rate 100-120 and breaths at rate of 10
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Firm surface (compression board on a bed); lower half of sternum; depth 1/3 of the AP diameter.**
claims.source_text: Place child on a firm surface. If on a bed, place cardiac compression board under child Perform chest compressions to lower half of sternum, compress by 1/3 of the AP diameter of the chest
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Infants: two-thumb encircling hold** (two-finger for a lone rescuer). **Children: heel of one hand**, or two hands.
claims.source_text: Infants: The recommended technique is a two-handed hold in which both thumbs compress the sternum The two-finger technique may be preferred by a single rescuer to minimise transition time between breaths and compressions. … Children: Chest compressions can be performed using the heel of one hand Two-handed technique can also be used
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not interrupt CPR except for a rhythm check or shock. Swap compressors every 2 minutes.**
claims.source_text: DO NOT interrupt CPR except for rhythm check or defibrillation Frequent changes of cardiac compression personnel (every 2 minutes) is desirable to avoid inadequate compressions due to fatigue
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **VF and pulseless VT: asynchronous shock at 4 J/kg (round up).** Charge while compressions continue.
claims.source_text: Minimise interruptions to CPR by charging whist chest compressions continue … DC shocks for VF and pulseless VT should be delivered asynchronously at a dose of 4 J/kg (round up)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Manual defibrillator preferred.** Standard AED is fine over 8 years; **under 8 years: manual, then AED with paediatric attenuation, then standard AED.**
claims.source_text: Manual defibrillators are preferred in infants and children. Standard AEDs can be used for children >8 years. For children <8 years, the order of preference is: Manual defibrillator AED with paediatric attenuation Standard AED
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Nobody touching the child when shocking** (COACHED). **After a shock, resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes before the next rhythm check.**
claims.source_text: Take care to ensure no one is touching the child at the time of delivering shock … If DC shock delivered, recommence CPR immediately for 2 minutes prior to rhythm check
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Adrenaline (1:10,000) 10 microg/kg = 0.1 mL/kg IV or intraosseous, max 1 mg.** (The page also lists IM here, which is not restated — see Unresolved.)
claims.source_text: Primary resuscitation drugs are: Adrenaline (1:10,000) 10 microg/kg = 0.1 mL/kg IV/IM/intraosseous (max 1 mg)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Amiodarone 5 mg/kg IV/intraosseous, max 300 mg — rapid bolus with 5% glucose.**
claims.source_text: Amiodarone 5 mg/kg IV/intraosseous (max 300 mg) -- deliver as a rapid bolus with 5% glucose
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Hypovolaemia: IV/IO crystalloid bolus 10–20 mL/kg**, further boluses titrated to response. **Hypoglycaemia: IV/IO 10% glucose 2 mL/kg**, aiming for normoglycaemia.
claims.source_text: Correct hypovolaemia: IV/IO crystalloid bolus of 10-20 mL/kg Additional bolus should be titrated to response … Correct hypoglycaemia: Aim for normoglycaemia IV/IO 10% glucose 2 mL/kg
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Atropine, lidocaine, sodium bicarbonate and calcium are not routine** — specific situations only.
claims.source_text: Atropine, lidocaine, sodium bicarbonate and calcium are not routinely used and should only be considered in specific situations
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Address the 4 Hs and 4 Ts:** hypoxaemia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperthermia, hypo/hyperkalaemia; tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis.
claims.source_text: Address reversible causes: 4 Hs and 4 Ts Hypoxaemia Hypovolaemia Hypo/hyperthermia Hypo/hyperkalaemia Tension pneumothorax Tamponade Toxins Thrombosis
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **ECPR is offered by specialised PICUs in Australia — consider it early** and discuss urgently with retrieval or onsite services.
claims.source_text: ECPR is a procedure offered by specialised paediatric intensive care centres in Australia … This should be considered early, within a short period of cardiopulmonary arrest and urgently discussed with appropriate local retrieval or onsite services
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Stopping CPR must involve experienced senior clinicians**, the clinical context and the family.
claims.source_text: The decision to cease CPR in children is difficult and must involve experienced senior clinicians, consider the clinical context, and occur in discussion with the child's family
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Admit to PICU.** Re-evaluate ABCD, do a 12-lead ECG and monitor for arrhythmias.
claims.source_text: Children resuscitated from a cardiorespiratory arrest should be admitted to PICU Ongoing reevaluation of ABCD Perform 12 lead ECG and monitor for arrhythmias
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Targets:** SpO2 94–98% (or PaO2 60–80 mmHg) · PaCO2 35–45 mmHg · systolic BP above the 10th percentile for age (50th percentile height), with inotropes as needed · glucose 4–8 mmol/L · **avoid hyperthermia**.
claims.source_text: Titrate inspired oxygen to achieve normal saturations: 94-98% or PaO2 60-80 mmHg) … Aim for normal CO2 levels: PaCO2 35-45 mmHg … Maintain systolic blood pressure >10th percentile for age and 50th percentile height with use of inotropes as needed … (avoid hyperthermia) … Maintain normoglycemia: 4-8 mmol/L
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Offer family presence** with a support person, and **debriefing and support for staff**, immediately and ongoing.
claims.source_text: Family members of children undergoing CPR should be offered to be present, ideally with an assigned support person … Debriefing and support should be offered to all involved staff who wish to attend both immediately post resuscitation and ongoing as required.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Resuscitation: hospital management of cardiopulmonary arrest' (Last updated December 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Resuscitation__hospital_management_of_cardiopulmonary_arrest/, retrieved 2026-09-23
